before: Any list that names a roughly equal number of events in each factor-of-ten interval of the past gives the same line, whether or not anything accelerated.
after: A list sampled roughly evenly within each factor-of-ten interval can produce a similar trend without any underlying acceleration; equal counts alone do not force exact collinearity or a particular fitted slope.

before: If events are sampled with density proportional to $t^{-k}$ in time-before-present $t$, the expected spacing near $t$ is the reciprocal of the density, so $\Delta t \propto t^{k}$ and the log–log plot has slope $k$. A list with equal numbers per decade has $k = 1$; a uniform sample in linear time has $k = 0$, a flat plot.
after: For many independently sampled events with density proportional to $t^{-k}$ in time-before-present $t$, a local typical spacing is approximately reciprocal to the event density where that density varies little across a gap and endpoints are negligible. Thus $\Delta t$ has a local scale proportional to $t^k$, suggesting a log–log trend of slope near $k$, not an exact expected finite-sample regression slope. Sampling uniformly in log time has $k=1$ and equal expected counts in equal log intervals; uniform sampling in linear time has $k=0$. Finite lists, boundary gaps and clustering can change the fitted slope.

before: Then switch to random events with sampling density ∝ t⁻ᵏ: with k = 1 (equal numbers per decade) pure noise gives the same straight line of slope ≈ 1, and with k = 0 (uniform in time) the line goes flat. The lower panel counts events per decade, which is what sets the slope.
after: Then switch to random events with sampling density ∝ t⁻ᵏ. For k = 1, equal log intervals have equal expected counts; the local typical-gap heuristic suggests a slope near 1. For k = 0 the density is uniform in linear time, suggesting locally constant gaps. The finite fitted slope can differ in either case. The lower panel shows the realized counts per decade; those counts alone do not determine the fitted slope.
